q: Hoisting means JavaScript moves your code to the top of the file before it runs.
why: No. Your code stays where it is. JavaScript only makes a slot in memory for every name before line 1 runs.
The slot for `a` was made before line 1 and started as `undefined`. Reading it early gives a quiet `undefined`, not an error.
A `let` slot starts locked. Reading it before its line throws a `ReferenceError`, and nobody catches it, so lines 2 and 3 never run.

q: Which of these slots start **locked** before line 1 runs?
why: `let` and `const` start locked (the temporal dead zone). `var` starts as `undefined`, and a function declaration starts as the whole function.

q: A function declaration written at the bottom of a file can be called from the top of the file.
why: Yes. The slot of a function declaration holds the whole function from the start, so it works anywhere in its scope.
Only the name `greet` was made early, as `undefined`. Calling `undefined` is a `TypeError`. A function expression in a `var` is not hoisted whole.

q: What does `show()` print? Type the one word.
why: The `var x` inside `show` makes a new slot at the start of `show`, holding `undefined`. It hides the outer `x` for the whole function, even in the line above it.

q: JavaScript looks for a name from the inside out. Put the places in the order it searches.
items: The block, inside the curly braces
why: It stops at the first room that has the name. If no room has it, the result is a `ReferenceError`.

q: Which of these statements are true?
options: `var` leaks out of the curly braces of an `if` or a `for`
`let` and `const` stay inside the nearest curly braces
A `var` slot starts locked until its line runs
why: `var` belongs to the function, so it ignores curly braces. `let` and `const` belong to the block. A `var` starts as `undefined`, not locked. `const` only locks the name.

q: What does this print? Type the three numbers with spaces between them.
why: `var` makes ONE `i` for the whole function. The timers run after the loop is done, when `i` is already 3.

q: The loop above prints `3 3 3`. Which one change makes it print `0 1 2`?
why: With `let`, each pass of the loop gets its own `i`, and each timer callback remembers its own. This is a closure (lesson 05).
No. `const` protects the name `user` (the arrow), not the inside of the object. Only `user = {}` would throw.

q: Which is the simple rule for new code?
options: Use `const` by default, `let` when the value must change, and not `var`
Use `var` everywhere, because it is the oldest and works
Use `let` for everything, and `const` only for numbers
Use `var` for functions and `const` for text
why: `const` and `let` stay inside the block and fail loudly when read too early. You still need to read `var`, because old code is full of it.
